\chapter{Carrying, Buying, Waiting, Meeting}
\label{ch:it-carry-buy-wait-meet}
\hlchaptermodality{20}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say in Italian that I carry or bring something, buy it, wait for someone and meet them, run all four through the -are endings without a pronoun, and put them into the past with avere rather than essere.}

The chapter's last lesson runs porto, compro, aspetto and incontro in one breath, then settles Chapter 16's open question by putting incontrare into the past: ho incontrato Marco and ho incontrato Anna, one unmoved participle, because only essere makes it agree — and it names the weld the other three share, a plain Latin verb behind com-, ad- and in-.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[portare]{portare — \textquotedblleft{}to carry,\textquotedblright{} and what an Italian does with a coat}

\label{lesson:IT-C20-portare}



\begin{quote}
Chapter 19 closed on a verb that ran backwards — \textbf{mi piace il vino}, where the wine does the pleasing and you are only the one it happens to. Here is a plain one: the \emph{-are} endings of \emph{aiuto, aiuti, aiuta}, doing a job English splits three ways.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{portare} — to carry, to bring, to take along.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Porto il pane.} — I bring the bread. \textbf{Porto l'acqua.} — I bring the water. \textbf{Porto il vino.} — I bring the wine.
\end{quote}

Hold it against \emph{prendere}, which was \textbf{seizing} — what you reach out and pick up. \emph{Portare} is what happens next: the thing travels with you.

A second job catches learners out. This same verb also means \textbf{to wear}. Clothes are things you carry on your person, so \emph{porto} covers a coat as readily as a loaf.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{portare} comes from Latin \textbf{portāre}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}to carry.\textquotedblright{}} English is stacked with it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{portable}; \textbf{porter}, who carries your bags; \textbf{portfolio}, from Italian \emph{portafoglio}, a leaf-carrier.
  \item \textbf{transport} (\textquotedblleft{}carry across\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{export} (\textquotedblleft{}carry out\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{import} (\textquotedblleft{}carry in\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{report} (\textquotedblleft{}carry back\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{support}, \textbf{deport}.
  \item \textbf{sport} — nobody sees this one coming. Old French \textbf{desporter} meant \textquotedblleft{}to carry away\textquotedblright{}: the mind, from serious matters. English wore \emph{disport} down to \textbf{sport}.
\end{itemize}

Two cautions. The harbour \textbf{port} is a different Latin word, \emph{portus}. And Latin \emph{manus}, which gave you \textbf{la mano}, sits in the phrase \emph{a mano}, \textquotedblleft{}by hand\textquotedblright{}: the hand is what does the carrying.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the endings, and a participle that behaves}]
Drop \emph{-are}, add the usual: \textbf{porto, porti, porta}.

Chapter 15 gave you \emph{ho} plus a participle; Chapters 18 and 19 handed you three that would not sit still. This one behaves:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{participle} & \textbf{with \emph{ho}} \\
\midrule
portare & \textbf{portato} & \textbf{ho portato} — I brought \\
scrivere & \emph{scritto} & \emph{ho scritto} — I wrote \\
prendere & \emph{preso} & \emph{ho preso} — I took \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Every regular \emph{-are} participle ends in \textbf{-ato}. \emph{Scritto} doubled its \emph{t} because \emph{scriptum} had a cluster to resolve; \emph{preso} lost an \emph{n} because \emph{prehēnsum} had one to lose. \emph{Portāre} had neither.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}porto, porti, porta\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Porto il pane. Porto l'acqua. Porto il vino.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}Ho portato il pane.\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Ho preso il pane.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}portare\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}transport, export, import, porter\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Bring the wine. (\emph{Porto il vino}.) What did \emph{portāre} mean, and name three English cousins. (\textbf{To carry}; \emph{transport, export, import, porter}.) Which English word for games is this verb in disguise? (\emph{Sport}, from \emph{desporter}, \textquotedblleft{}to carry away\textquotedblright{}.) Give the participle, and say why it is not doubled like \emph{scritto}. (\emph{Portato}; \emph{portāre} had no cluster to collapse.) What else does \emph{portare} mean? (\textbf{To wear}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[comprare]{comprare — \textquotedblleft{}to buy,\textquotedblright{} and the false trail to \textquotedblleft{}compare\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:IT-C20-comprare}



\begin{quote}
A second \emph{-are} verb, so the endings cost you nothing. What is new is the root, which sends nearly every English speaker down the wrong road on sight.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{comprare} — to buy.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Compro il pane.} — I buy the bread. \textbf{Compro l'acqua.} — I buy the water. \textbf{Compro il vino.} — I buy the wine.
\end{quote}

Italian keeps a longer form too, \textbf{comperare}. That is the older shape; speech squeezed the middle \emph{e} out. Both are real, and the short one is what you hear.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{comprare} comes from Latin \textbf{comparāre}, and the verb underneath it is \textbf{parāre}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}to make ready, to procure.\textquotedblright{}} Put \textbf{com-}, \textquotedblleft{}together,\textquotedblright{} in front and buying is \textbf{procuring}: bringing the thing and the price into one place. English took \emph{parāre} over and over:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{prepare} (\emph{prae-}, \textquotedblleft{}beforehand\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{repair} (\emph{re-}, \textquotedblleft{}back into readiness\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{separate} (\emph{sē-}, \textquotedblleft{}apart\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{apparatus} and \textbf{apparel} — things made ready, for a machine and for a body.
  \item \textbf{emperor} and \textbf{empire}, through \emph{imperāre}, which is \emph{in-} plus this same \emph{parāre}.
  \item Italian's own \textbf{parare}, \textquotedblleft{}to ward off,\textquotedblright{} borrowed as \textbf{parry} and standing in \textbf{parasol} and \textbf{parachute}.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
English \textbf{compare} looks like a free gift here. It is not: the resemblance is exact and the connection is nil. Latin had \textbf{two} verbs spelled \emph{comparāre}, built on unrelated words:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Latin verb} & \textbf{built on} & \textbf{where it went} \\
\midrule
\emph{comparāre} (procure) & \emph{parāre}, \textquotedblleft{}make ready\textquotedblright{} & Italian \textbf{comprare}, to buy \\
\emph{comparāre} (match) & \emph{pār}, \textquotedblleft{}equal\textquotedblright{} & English \textbf{compare} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The second is the \emph{pār} of \textbf{par}, \textbf{parity}, \textbf{peer}, \textbf{pair} and \textbf{umpire}: setting two things side by side as equals. Buying is procuring, not weighing up.

\textbf{Spanish} \emph{comprar} and \textbf{Portuguese} \emph{comprar} took the procuring-verb Italian took; \textbf{French} abandoned it and buys with \emph{acheter}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: run them together}]
Chapter 5's exercise still works, with more to chew on. Take each \emph{-are} verb through \emph{io / tu / lui-lei}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{parlare}: parlo · parli · parla
  \item \textbf{portare}: porto · porti · porta
  \item \textbf{comprare}: compro · compri · compra
\end{itemize}

Same three endings, \textbf{-o / -i / -a}, and the pronoun stays dropped. The past is regular: \textbf{ho comprato il pane}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}compro, compri, compra\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Compro il pane. Compro il vino.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the run — \textquotedblleft{}parlo, porto, compro\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}comprare\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}prepare, repair, separate, apparatus\textquotedblright{}
  \item the warning — \textquotedblleft{}\emph{comprare} is procuring, \textbf{not} comparing\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Buy the bread. (\emph{Compro il pane}.) Which Latin verb is inside \emph{comprare}? (\emph{Parāre} — \textbf{to make ready, to procure}.) Name three English cousins. (\emph{Prepare, repair, separate, apparatus, emperor}.) Why is English \emph{compare} \textbf{not} a relative? (Different Latin verb, same spelling, built on \emph{pār}, \textquotedblleft{}equal\textquotedblright{}.) And which verb from the last lesson meant \textquotedblleft{}to carry\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Portare}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aspettare]{aspettare — \textquotedblleft{}to wait,\textquotedblright{} which began as \textquotedblleft{}to watch\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:IT-C20-aspettare}



\begin{quote}
A third \emph{-are} verb. Its endings are free, its root is one of the most productive in English, and the doubled \emph{tt} in the middle is the work of a sound-law you learned while counting to ten.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{aspettare} — to wait, to wait \textbf{for}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Aspetto.} — I'm waiting. \textbf{Aspetto Anna.} — I'm waiting for Anna. \textbf{Aspetto Marco.} — I'm waiting for Marco.
\end{quote}

Notice what the Italian is missing: any word meaning \textbf{for}. English cannot \textquotedblleft{}wait somebody.\textquotedblright{} Italian takes the person straight, as \emph{porto il pane} takes the bread.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{aspettare} comes from Latin \textbf{spectāre}, \emph{\textquotedblleft{}to watch, to gaze at\textquotedblright{}}, with \textbf{ad-}, \textquotedblleft{}toward,\textquotedblright{} welded on the front: to watch \textbf{toward} something. Waiting is watching for a thing to arrive, and the root runs through English:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{spectator}, \textbf{spectacle}, \textbf{spectacles}, \textbf{spectrum}.
  \item \textbf{inspect} (\textquotedblleft{}look into\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{respect} (\textquotedblleft{}look back at\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{prospect} (\textquotedblleft{}look forward\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{suspect} (\textquotedblleft{}look from underneath\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{aspect}.
  \item \textbf{species} and \textbf{specimen}, from the plain verb \emph{specere}, \textquotedblleft{}to look.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

Classical Latin's own word for waiting was \textbf{exspectāre} — \emph{ex-} plus that same verb, \textquotedblleft{}to watch out for\textquotedblright{} — and English took \textbf{that} one and made it \textbf{expect}. So \emph{wait} and \emph{expect} are one Latin verb wearing two prefixes, and Italian's single \emph{aspettare} stands on the ground of both.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the doubled t, and the word that narrows the meaning}]
Present: \textbf{aspetto, aspetti, aspetta}. Past: \textbf{ho aspettato}, regular.

First that \emph{tt}. Latin \emph{spectāre} carries \emph{-ct-}, and you know what Italian does with \emph{-ct-}: \emph{octō} became \textbf{otto}, \emph{lectum} \textbf{letto}, \emph{scriptum} \textbf{scritto}. The same law gives \textbf{aspettare}.

Second, the narrowing. Put \textbf{mi} in front and the verb stops meaning \emph{wait} and starts meaning \emph{expect}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Italian} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Aspetto.} & I'm waiting. \\
\textbf{Mi aspetto.} & I expect. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That \textbf{mi} is a word you have met working elsewhere. In \textbf{mi chiamo} it turned the verb back on you — \textquotedblleft{}I call \emph{myself}.\textquotedblright{} In \textbf{mi piace} it named the person a thing is pleasing \emph{to}. Here it turns outward watching into inward reckoning.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}aspetto, aspetti, aspetta\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Aspetto Anna.\textquotedblright{} — no word for \emph{for}
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}Aspetto.\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Mi aspetto.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three uses of \emph{mi} — \textquotedblleft{}mi chiamo, mi piace, mi aspetto\textquotedblright{}
  \item the law — \textquotedblleft{}\emph{octō} $\to$ otto, \emph{scriptum} $\to$ scritto, \emph{spectāre} $\to$ aspettare\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say you are waiting for Anna. (\emph{Aspetto Anna} — nothing for \textquotedblleft{}for\textquotedblright{}.) What did \emph{spectāre} mean, and name three English cousins. (\textbf{To watch}; \emph{spectator, inspect, respect, prospect, species}.) Which prefix gave English \emph{expect}, and which gave Italian \emph{aspettare}? (\emph{Ex-} and \emph{ad-}.) Why the doubled \emph{tt}, and what does \textbf{mi aspetto} mean? (\emph{-ct-} collapses to \emph{-tt-}, as in \emph{otto}; \textbf{I expect}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[incontrare]{incontrare — \textquotedblleft{}to meet,\textquotedblright{} which is literally \textquotedblleft{}to come against\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:IT-C20-incontrare}



\begin{quote}
The chapter's last \emph{-are} verb. Its root is a preposition, its past settles a question Chapter 16 left open, and Italian keeps a second meeting-verb that shows its meaning only in the past.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{incontrare} — to meet, to run into. \textbf{incontro, incontri, incontra}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Incontro Marco.} — I meet Marco. \textbf{Incontro Anna.} — I meet Anna.
\end{quote}

It has a partner English cannot keep apart from it, \textbf{conoscere}. \emph{Incontrare} is the \textbf{event}, two people in one place; \emph{conoscere} is the \textbf{acquaintance}, knowing a person.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{incontrare} $\leftarrow$ Late Latin \textbf{incontrā}: \textbf{in-} plus \textbf{contrā}, \textquotedblleft{}against, opposite.\textquotedblright{} To meet somebody is to come \emph{against} them — not a fight, a facing. English borrowed it through French as \textbf{encounter}; bare \emph{contrā} gave \textbf{contrary}, \textbf{contrast}, \textbf{counter}.

The best of the family is \textbf{country}: Vulgar Latin named a region \emph{(terra) contrāta}, \textquotedblleft{}the land lying opposite\textquotedblright{} — what is in front of you when you turn from the town.

\textbf{conoscere} is a different house: Latin \textbf{cognōscere}, \emph{co-} plus \emph{gnōscere}, \textquotedblleft{}to come to know\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textbf{cognition}, \textbf{recognize}, \textbf{incognito}, \textbf{notice}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: which past, and the one that means \textquotedblleft{}met\textquotedblright{}}]
Chapter 16 split the past in two. Motion and change take \textbf{essere}, and the participle agrees: \emph{Marco è andato}, \emph{Anna è andata}, \emph{sono stato}. All else takes \textbf{avere}, and nothing agrees.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ho incontrato Marco.} — I met Marco. \textbf{Ho incontrato Anna.} — I met Anna.
\end{quote}

Two people, one unmoved \textbf{incontrato} — because after \emph{essere} the participle began as an adjective describing the subject, and after \emph{avere} it describes nobody.

Now the hidden verb. Put \textbf{conoscere} in the past and its job changes:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ho conosciuto Marco.} — I met Marco — for the first time.
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{portare} $\leftarrow$ \emph{portāre}, \textquotedblleft{}carry\textquotedblright{} $\to$ transport, export, porter, \emph{sport}; it also means to \textbf{wear}, and \emph{portato} is the regular participle.
  \item \textbf{comprare} $\leftarrow$ \emph{comparāre} on \emph{parāre}, \textquotedblleft{}procure\textquotedblright{} $\to$ prepare, repair, apparatus — and \textbf{not} the \emph{comparāre} behind English \emph{compare}.
  \item \textbf{aspettare} $\leftarrow$ \emph{ad-} + \emph{spectāre}, \textquotedblleft{}watch toward\textquotedblright{} $\to$ spectator, inspect, prospect; \emph{ex-} on that verb gave \emph{expect}, and \textbf{mi aspetto} says it.
  \item \textbf{incontrare} $\leftarrow$ \emph{in-} + \emph{contrā}, \textquotedblleft{}against\textquotedblright{} $\to$ encounter, contrary, country.
  \item \textbf{The thread}: four verbs, one set of \emph{-are} endings — \emph{porto, compro, aspetto, incontro} — and three of them weld a small word onto a plain Latin verb: \emph{com-}, \emph{ad-}, \emph{in-}. Italian inherited the welds without the seams.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Incontro Marco. Ho incontrato Anna.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the contrast — \textquotedblleft{}Anna è andata\textquotedblright{} beside \textquotedblleft{}Ho incontrato Anna\textquotedblright{}
  \item the first meeting — \textquotedblleft{}Ho conosciuto Marco.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the chapter — \textquotedblleft{}porto, compro, aspetto, incontro\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Meet Marco. (\emph{Incontro Marco}.) What two pieces make \emph{incontrā}, and which English word for a place is \emph{contrā} in disguise? (\emph{In-} plus \emph{contrā}; \emph{country}.) Why \emph{ho incontrato Anna} and not \emph{sono incontrata}? (Not motion, so \emph{avere}.) Name the roots under the chapter's other three verbs. (\emph{Portāre}, \emph{parāre}, \emph{spectāre}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
